expr: (list (progn (string-match "foo" "Foo bar") (replace-match "baz" nil t "Foo bar")) (progn (string-match "foo" "FOO bar") (replace-match "baz" nil t "FOO bar")) (progn (string-match "foo" "FOO bar") (replace-match "baz" t t "FOO bar")))
note: FIXEDCASE, both ways round, on the two cases the argument exists for. Emacs answers ("Baz bar" "BAZ bar" "baz bar"): with FIXEDCASE nil a capitalised match capitalises the replacement and an upcased match upcases it, and with FIXEDCASE t the replacement goes in verbatim. The subject strings are chosen so the MATCH ITSELF is already in the string -- kg folds no case, so a pattern that needed folding to match would be measuring a different divergence (phase15-replace-regexp-case is that one). THE SUBJECT-CHOICE CLAIM ABOVE IS WRONG, and 26.2 found it by running the case: "foo" does not match "Foo bar" or "FOO bar" WITHOUT case folding, which is the very thing kg does not have. So all three elements fail at `string-match', the register stays empty, and kg raises `replace-match subexpression does not exist' rather than answering a string. This case therefore CANNOT agree until kg has `case-fold-search', whatever `replace-match' does with FIXEDCASE, which is why it keeps the divergence inside an otherwise-agreeing row. 26.2's decision on the argument itself: DECLINED, kg's `replace-match' accepts FIXEDCASE and ignores it exactly as `replace-regexp-in-string' beside it does, so the two names do not disagree about one argument -- the shape Phase 25.2 resolved for `string=' against `string<'. Recorded against phase26-replace-match-case-conversion.
